video_title: Dan Niles: The AI Trade Has a Cisco Problem
gist: Dan Niles (Niles Investment Management) tells Dan Nathan he is tactically cautious on equities because the Fed is in a hiking cycle, the 10-year is near 5%, and September/midterm-year seasonality is the worst of the calendar — while the AI trade faces a political data-center backlash (Texas moratorium), frontier labs publicly talking about 'pacing' innovation, collapsing per-token pricing and volume migrating to open-weight models. He invokes Cisco's May 2001 press release — when orders flipped from roughly +50% year-over-year to -30% in months — as the template for why today's hundreds-of-billions AI backlogs are unreliable, but still puts himself in the 'speed bump, not the top' camp with one to two years left in the agentic AI cycle. On single names he is constructive on Meta (dark horse), Google, Microsoft/Copilot and Apple's 2027 foldable upgrade cycle.

insights.claim: Dan Niles is tactically cautious on US equities because three historically reliable forces — the Fed, the bond market and seasonality — are aligned against stocks at the same time, a combination he says he will not fight.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A framework for sizing down risk rather than picking a top: when all three signals agree, reduce net exposure instead of waiting for a fundamental catalyst.
insights.quote: right now I feel like you have all three of those things between the Fed, the bond market, and seasonality

insights.claim: September is the only month since 1957 (the inception of the modern S&P) that is down on average and down more often than it is up, which Niles uses as a standing reason to de-risk into the month.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A repeatable calendar overlay: seasonality argues for lighter equity exposure in September regardless of the fundamental narrative.
insights.quote: September being the only month since 1957 that's down on average and um is uh down more often than it's up

insights.claim: In midterm election years the average S&P 500 peak-to-trough drawdown from July 31st to November 9th has been roughly 10% since 1990 — double the equivalent non-midterm-year drawdown — and the market is nowhere near that this cycle.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Implies unrealized downside into early November; a reason to buy downside protection rather than chase an index within 2% of all-time highs.
insights.quote: The average draw down from July 31st to to November 9th is about 10% from peak to trough in the S&P. That's double what it is in non-midterm years.

insights.claim: Niles expects the Fed to skip the October meeting because it falls roughly five days before the midterms and the White House blowback would be severe, but sees the December 10th meeting as a live hike.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Positions December, not October, as the rates event risk; options and rate-sensitive positioning should be built around the December meeting.
insights.quote: I doubt the Fed's going to want to raise right in front of the elections because the amount of blowback they're going to get from the White House would be ridiculous

insights.claim: Because inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for 65 consecutive months, a single quarter-point hike accomplishes nothing and investors should expect a series of rate hikes rather than a one-and-done move.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Markets historically underperform during hiking cycles; pricing a single hike rather than a sequence is the mispricing to fade.
insights.quote: inflation's been running above the 2% target now for 65 months actually with now it might be 66 and so like we're nowhere close and so you you should expect a series of rate hikes

insights.claim: The unanimous Fed vote to raise 25 basis points surprised Niles, who expected at least one dissent, and he flags that the hiking cycle is synchronized globally across Japan, the ECB and the UK rather than being a US-only phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A globally synchronized tightening removes the offshore liquidity bid that has historically cushioned US equity drawdowns.
insights.quote: That shocked me. It was unanimous. I thought there'd be at least one descent

insights.claim: Hyperscalers that historically never needed external capital are now raising debt and equity and therefore competing directly with a US federal government running a 6% deficit-to-GDP — the largest non-wartime deficit on record — with Google having gone cash flow negative for the first time since its IPO.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Crowding-out risk: AI capex now has a rising cost of capital, which compresses the return math that justified the build-out at zero rates.
insights.quote: Google went cash flow negative for the first time since they went public. They're raising debt. They're raising equity.

insights.claim: With Japanese yields at their highest since the 1990s and US yields back to 2007-2008 levels, a guaranteed 5% ten-year return has become a genuine competitor to equities trading near their highest market-cap-to-GDP levels since 2000.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The equity risk premium is effectively gone; marginal savings flows can leave equities without any earnings disappointment at all.
insights.quote: a guaranteed 5% return over 10 years at these valuation levels, which you know on a debt on a GDP versus market cap basis, you're you're tracking to one of the highest levels since 2000

insights.claim: The yen carry trade — long called the widowmaker because shorting Japan never worked — has begun working over the past year, and a broader unwind would be a far bigger problem for US equities than valuations alone.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Watch JGB yields as the trigger for forced deleveraging of long-duration US assets, including the most crowded AI names.
insights.quote: they called it the widowmaker trade, right? Trying to short um Japan because it just hasn't worked. And now it's starting to really work over the last year or so.

insights.claim: Niles argues that the prevailing 'always buy the dip' reflex exists only because governments and central banks could throw money at every problem through COVID, and that with both now running out of ammunition the assumption that markets cannot stay down is unsafe.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Reflexive dip-buying is the consensus behavior most likely to be punished if policy support is genuinely constrained this cycle.
insights.quote: central banks and governments which are running up out of ammunition, which is part of the reason why the bond market's doing what it's doing, that creates an issue

themes.theme: Data Center Politics as the New Bear Catalyst

insights.claim: Texas — a deeply red, historically pro-data-center state and the second largest data center state behind West Virginia — imposed a moratorium on data center expansion and grid connections, which Niles cites as the event that turned him more negative on the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Political constraint on the build-out is now bipartisan and can throttle capex faster than any demand signal; track state-level utility and interconnection rulings as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: the state of Texas, which is a big proponent of data centers, they went ahead and started to put a moratorum on data center expansion essentially and connecting some of those data centers to the grid

insights.claim: Niles identifies a direct contradiction in the bull case: if power and land constraints are what cap AI spending, then bipartisan pushback on grid connections must by definition reduce total spend, so investors cannot use scarcity as a bullish argument and ignore permitting risk.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Exposes a logical flaw in the 'we can't overbuild' consensus — the same constraint that supports pricing also caps volume for suppliers.
insights.quote: That means by definition you're going to have less spend, right? You can't have it both ways.

insights.claim: Socialist Democrats picking up seats across multiple states run on a platform that is anti-big-business and specifically anti-data-center, so Niles questions his own prior assumption that markets get better after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Post-midterm relief may not arrive for AI infrastructure names; election outcomes are a fundamental input, not just a volatility event.
insights.quote: if you look at their platform, by definition, they are anti- big business and they're really anti- data centers

insights.claim: The semiconductor index is up over 60% year to date while representing only low-teens percent of the S&P 500, meaning the rest of the market has delivered minuscule returns and index performance is almost entirely an AI bet.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Index-level exposure is a concentrated AI position; any semiconductor de-rating flows straight through to benchmark returns with no offset.
insights.quote: if you look at the semiconductor index for the year, it's up over 60%. That's somewhere in the low teens percentage of the S&P 500.

insights.claim: AI capex grew roughly 75% last year and roughly 100% this year, and Niles argues the trade breaks on deceleration alone — the internet still doubled in 2001 and 2002, it just stopped doubling every three to six months.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The bear case does not require a demand collapse; second-derivative slowing is sufficient to de-rate suppliers, which makes capex growth rates the number to track.
insights.quote: it's not like the internet stopped growing in 2001 2002 it doubled in each of those years it's just it wasn't doubling every three three to six months so you don't need it to contract you just need the growth rates to slow

insights.claim: Niles' June 20th call that the AI trade would hit a speed bump was followed by semiconductors falling 29% from June 22nd to July 29th, a precedent he cites for how violently the group can correct without the secular story changing.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Establishes the realistic magnitude of an AI 'speed bump' — roughly 30% in semis — which is the drawdown to size positions against.
insights.quote: turned out semiconductors went down 29% from June 22nd to July 29th. So it was one heck of a speed bump.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan notes that semis are down 25% from July all-time highs even though the SOX doubled from April to June, and that Intel rallied 10% intraday on an SK Hynix headline about an Ohio fab that would not be built until roughly 2030 — evidence investors are trading pure headlines rather than cash flows.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Headline-driven 10% single-day moves in large caps signal positioning stress and favor volatility selling or tactical trading over buy-and-hold in semis.
insights.quote: Why would you afford this stock, that market cap right now based on that sort of headline?

themes.theme: Token Economics and the Open-Weight Migration

insights.claim: The average cost per token charged has fallen 50% from the end of May to today while the number of tokens produced quadrupled, so unit-volume growth has so far more than offset price deflation in AI inference.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The key AI revenue identity is volume times price; when the quadrupling stops outrunning the 50% price cuts, model-layer revenue growth inverts.
insights.quote: you've seen the cost per token being charged on average go down 50% since the end of May till today. The good news is that the number of tokens being produced quadrupled.

insights.claim: According to the Ramp index, the top 1% of AI users cut their spend 10% from July to August — the first decline after essentially straight-up monthly growth since ChatGPT launched — even as the other 99% kept increasing spend.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Heaviest users are the leading indicator; a rollover at the top of the spend curve typically precedes broader deceleration in AI subscription and API revenue.
insights.quote: the top 1% of users they actually saw a 10% reduction in spend from July to August if you look at the ramp index

insights.claim: Customers are deliberately downgrading from expensive frontier models to cheap open-source open-weight models, which Niles frames as realizing they had been using a Ferrari to drive to the corner store for milk when a Ford would do.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Model commoditization compresses the frontier labs' pricing power and the downstream compute intensity assumed in hyperscaler capex plans.
insights.quote: we've been using a Ferrari to go to the corner store to get milk and we should be using a Ford

insights.claim: Token volume is increasingly accruing to the open-weight model group — mostly Chinese models plus US entrants like Nemotron and Meta's newly launched model — meaning AI revenue growth is real but landing outside the closed frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Bullish for compute and for Meta's distribution, bearish for the private frontier labs' valuations that assume they capture the inference economics.
insights.quote: thankfully the one metric underneath it which is revenue growth seems to be working. The bad news is a lot of that seems to be acrewing to open source.

insights.claim: OpenAI sharply cut the price of its leading models and appears to be taking share from Anthropic as a result, but its profitability metrics reportedly got worse — a data point Niles caveats as secondhand because both companies are private.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Share gains bought with price cuts at deteriorating margins is the classic pre-consolidation pattern; relevant to how public-market investors should price the eventual OpenAI IPO.
insights.quote: Looks like they're taking a lot of share as a result from Anthropic, but as a result of that, it seems like the profitability metrics are getting worse.

insights.claim: Architectural shifts such as separating the cache from the inference step may reduce the compute required per unit of AI output, adding a third structural headwind alongside data center politics and model-price deflation.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains at the architecture layer undercut the linear compute-demand extrapolations embedded in semi and data-center estimates unless Jevons paradox keeps holding.
insights.quote: You better hope that that Jevans paradox which everybody keeps quoting continues.

themes.theme: The Cisco 2001 Template and Backlog Skepticism

insights.claim: Niles points to Cisco's May 2001 earnings press release, in which orders swung from roughly up 50% year-over-year to down roughly 30% within several months, as the historical proof that hardware backlogs can evaporate almost instantly.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete precedent and a checkable document for how fast an AI order book could reverse; argues against paying up for backlog-based valuations.
insights.quote: they went from orders being up 50% year-over-year to down 30 in several months

insights.claim: The hundreds of billions of dollars in announced AI backlogs are unreliable because scarcity induces customers to double and triple order, and Niles doubts a meaningful share will be realized over the next five years.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Discount headline backlog numbers when valuing suppliers; the order book is the most inflated input in current AI models.
insights.quote: this backlog stuff is ridiculous because I go it can change. you can change very quickly. And when you can't get what you want anyway, you're going to double and triple order.

insights.claim: Niles believes overbuilding is the rational and inevitable consequence of AI being genuinely transformational, citing Satya Nadella's stated view that the biggest risk is underinvesting rather than overinvesting.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Overbuild is a feature of the cycle, not evidence the thesis is wrong — but it guarantees casualties among second-tier suppliers even if the winners compound.
insights.quote: The biggest risk is underinvesting, not overinvesting.

insights.claim: Niles expects AI to produce dot-com-style train wrecks alongside eventual dominant winners, citing AOL, Webvan and Pets.com as failures against Google, Meta and an Amazon that fell 95% before becoming the dominant e-commerce platform.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Even correct secular theses produce 90%+ drawdowns in the eventual winners; position sizing and entry price matter more than being right on the theme.
insights.quote: Web Van certainly didn't make it. Neither did Pest.com, but Amazon stock went down 95%. But ultimately, it came out of that.

insights.claim: Despite the bearish inputs, Niles explicitly puts himself in the 'speed bump' rather than 'we have seen the top' camp, arguing the agentic AI trade only began on January 30th with OpenClaw and has at least another year or two to run.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The call is tactical de-risking inside an intact secular bull, which argues for buying drawdowns rather than shorting the theme outright.
insights.quote: I think we're just so early in the agentic AI trade which really started only on January 30th with OpenClaw that I feel like we still have at least a year or two to run

insights.claim: Niles notes Nvidia would look ridiculously cheap at a mid-teens multiple on calendar 2027 earnings if estimates prove right, but warns entire sub-sectors such as memory may be over-earning, so the cheap multiple may be on peak numbers.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The 'cheap on out-year estimates' argument is the AI bull case's weakest link; stress-test the denominator before treating semis as value.
insights.quote: if the estimates are right, this thing is ridiculously cheap, trading at a mid- teens multiple for calendar 27, you know, earnings. But you also go, well, are a lot of companies over earning, such as in memory

themes.theme: Frontier Lab Motives and Circular Financing

insights.claim: Niles reads the recent calls by Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk to slow the pace of AI innovation as three simultaneous true motives: genuine safety concern, a desire for a government-sanctioned duopoly that chokes off open-weight competitors, and a cleaner cash-flow profile ahead of OpenAI and Anthropic going public.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Treat safety rhetoric from frontier labs as competitive and IPO positioning; regulatory capture of open-weight models would reprice the entire open-source-exposed stack.
insights.quote: remember two things can be true at once. You can be concerned about what this technology can do and at the same time you can be wanting to have a government sanctioned duopoly if you can

insights.claim: Niles does not believe any frontier lab can actually slow spending, because if one paces itself while Google keeps going it gets left behind — though a pre-IPO company might slow for a quarter or two purely to flatter cash flow and expenses.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Discount slowdown talk as durable guidance; a temporary optical pause around an IPO is the realistic scenario and would still hit suppliers' near-term orders.
insights.quote: if you slow down and Google keeps going, you're spooked. So, I don't think any of these companies is actually going to slow down

insights.claim: Circular financing among Microsoft, OpenAI, Nvidia and Oracle does not matter until spending slows, exactly as circular vendor financing in the 1990s was ignored until Cisco suffered at least two separate 30%-plus drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Circularity is a fragility amplifier, not a timing signal; use capex deceleration rather than deal structure as the trigger to act on it.
insights.quote: the circular financing stuff's only going to matter when things start to slow

themes.theme: Who Actually Wins: Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft

insights.claim: Anthropic is now larger than OpenAI on revenue — roughly $65 billion versus $40 billion on the latest available figures — because it targeted enterprises from day one while OpenAI targeted consumers who do not pay.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Reverses the consensus ranking of the two labs and argues enterprise monetization, not consumer scale, is the durable AI business model.
insights.quote: The last figures we have is Anthropic's at 65 billion in revenues and Open AI is at 40 billion.

insights.claim: Anthropic reportedly reached adjusted operating profitability in Q2 with further improvement in Q3, a metric Niles flags as directionally positive while explicitly disliking the 'adjusted' framing.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: First credible profitability signal at the model layer; sets a benchmark for valuing OpenAI and for judging whether AI economics can work without subsidy.
insights.quote: They also have termed profitable adjusted operating profits and I hate that term, but that they supposedly got to adjusted profitability in Q2.

insights.claim: Google Cloud posted the sharpest acceleration of any hyperscaler — growth going from 63% to 82% versus AWS 28% to 37% and Azure 39% to 43% — and the stock failed to respond only because it reported before the 'situational awareness' unwind hit public portfolios.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Identifies a fundamentals-versus-price dislocation in Google driven by positioning timing rather than business performance — the setup Niles buys.
insights.quote: and GCP it went from growing 63 to 82%. The reason the stock didn't act well was they reported before situational awareness got bound down their public portfolio

insights.claim: Niles argues Google's durable edge is training data harvested from its free products, that Google invented the transformer technology OpenAI commercialized first, and that with Sergey Brin and Larry Page still intimately involved he expects Google back in the top model tier within months.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Treats Gemini's current frontier gap as temporary and mean-reverting; frontier leadership leapfrogs, so model benchmarks are a poor basis for long-term stock selection.
insights.quote: don't forget these guys invented the transformer technology that OpenAI went out and then commercialized first

insights.claim: Niles' dark horse is Meta: the Meta Agent is the number two downloaded free app behind ChatGPT, Meta has 3.6 billion daily active users, and the stock trades at a market multiple versus peers in the low 20s PE while being up only about 1% year to date.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A cheap, under-owned way to own consumer agentic AI distribution — the rare setup where valuation risk and AI upside are not in conflict.
insights.quote: it's sort of got the holy grail of it can be a value stock, a growth stock, and an AI play all at the same time

insights.claim: Meta is running the same playbook Google ran in 2025 — settle a legal overhang (the attorneys general settlement on youth safety), then ship strong products — which Niles says can re-rate a stock very quickly.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A repeatable screen: large-cap tech emerging from regulatory overhang with a product catalyst is a high-probability re-rating setup.
insights.quote: you settle an legal overhang and then you introducing good products, you can rewrite very quickly

insights.claim: Meta's Watermelon model, positioned to challenge at the frontier, is due out by October at the latest, with the Meta Connect conference the following week as a possible preview venue.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A dated, tradeable catalyst for Meta within weeks; frontier-parity confirmation would justify multiple expansion from a market multiple.
insights.quote: watermelon coming out which is their supposedly a model that's going to challenge at the frontier and that's going to be out at the latest in October

insights.claim: Microsoft rallied roughly 20% in a straight line after its print specifically because estimates went up while capex did not, in contrast to Google whose acceleration was ignored due to reporting before the unwind.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: The market is currently paying for capex discipline, not capex growth — a regime change that favors capex-light AI monetizers over builders.
insights.quote: well that's because they didn't raise capex

insights.claim: Microsoft has no need to spend on frontier model training because it is entitled to all of OpenAI's IP, having invested roughly $13 billion for 27% of the company while also being one of OpenAI's largest infrastructure vendors.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Microsoft gets frontier capability without frontier capex, which is the highest-quality structure in the AI stack if model prices keep deflating.
insights.quote: Why should they be spending money when open is meant spending a ton of money and they can get the IP for free

insights.claim: Copilot has 30 million users against Microsoft 365's 450 million enterprise seats, and Niles argues corporate fear of rogue agents — which he attributes to poor sandboxing by operators rather than agent misbehavior, citing the Hugging Face attack — could drive Copilot adoption toward the full base on security grounds.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Frames enterprise AI security as Microsoft's distribution moat and gives a 15x seat-penetration runway as the upside case.
insights.quote: They have 450 million. They've got 30 million of co-pilot and that's the real interesting part is co-pilot starting to ramp

insights.claim: Niles expects AI to consolidate to a few dominant players the way the internet did — Google in search, Amazon in e-commerce, Netflix in streaming, Meta in social — but notes that even three AI winners would be more than the internet produced per category.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Argues against owning a broad AI basket; the historical base rate says one or two names capture nearly all the category value.
insights.quote: I think this will end up being like every other major technological shift, which is ultimately it coaleses down to a few players.

themes.theme: Apple: Foldable Upgrade Cycle vs Capex-Light Defense

insights.claim: Niles explicitly disagrees with the premise that Apple needs Siri AI working to drive a new product cycle, arguing the foldable form factor is the actual catalyst — the analogue being the iPhone 6's move from a 4-inch to a 5.5-inch screen, which took revenue growth from 7% in fiscal 2014 to 28% in the following fiscal year.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Reframes the Apple debate away from AI capability toward hardware form factor, with a historical revenue-acceleration precedent to size the upgrade cycle.
insights.quote: You go back and you look at the iPhone 6 you move from 4 in to 5 1/2 in screen. Revenue growth went from 7% in fiscal 14 to 28% growth in fiscal 50.

insights.claim: Niles predicts a huge Apple upgrade cycle next year driven by older, affluent buyers whose eyesight favors a much bigger screen — a demographic he says has been waiting since Samsung shipped foldables in 2019.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, high-ASP buyer cohort as the demand source, which supports both unit and mix upside in Apple's next fiscal year.
insights.quote: I think you've got a lot of people with money who eyes aren't as young as they used to be

insights.claim: Niles warns Apple's near-term numbers could be too high because only the expensive Duo and Pro Max SKUs are available and the affordable base models do not arrive until the first half of next year, making the December quarter a risk.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Separates the timing of the trade from the thesis: the bullish foldable cycle is a next-year story with a potential estimate cut in between.
insights.quote: I think near-term numbers could be potentially too high because you don't have the base model phones for those people who can't afford paying $2,000 for the Duo or the Pro Pro Max, right?

insights.claim: Apple is defensive in a tightening environment precisely because it is not spending $200 billion a year on capex — it lets Google spend and licenses the model back for a couple of billion dollars a year, preserving massive free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: Makes Apple the natural hedge inside a tech book if AI capex decelerates or the cost of capital keeps rising.
insights.quote: the stock is very defensive when you're not spending 200 billion a year on capex. That's a pretty good pretty good deal in this environment.

insights.claim: Niles sees the leadership handoff to Ternus as a positive for product innovation, contrasting a product executive against Tim Cook, whom he credits with financial engineering and supply chain mastery that drove the multiple higher but not new categories.
insights.speaker: Dan Niles
insights.so_what: A management-driven re-rating argument for Apple that is independent of AI; watch the product cadence over the next few hardware launches as the test.
insights.quote: Tim Cook was great for financial engineering, supply chain management. He was a god and the multiple went up a a ton under his watch.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan argues the all-glass folding design threatens Apple's roughly 90% gross margin accessory business — 19 years of selling cases and screen protectors on billions of iPhones — and creates real 'antenna gate' style durability headline risk on a $2,400 device.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A specific, under-discussed margin and reputational risk in the foldable launch; a durability scandal would delay the upgrade cycle Niles is underwriting.
insights.quote: three quarters of that device are glass, okay? And it folds. And there's no way that you can put any sort of protection on this thing.
